slide.title: Built It or Bought It?
slide.body: One AI system box in the centre; left icon: builder with wrench (provider); right icon: buyer with bag (deployer). Small tag: AI Governance, Privacy and Compliance · Lesson 4.

scenes.voiceover: Two organisations use the same high-risk AI system. One built it. The other bought it. Do they have the same duties? No. Under the EU AI Act, your obligations depend on your role, and one organisation can hold several roles at once.

slide.title: EU AI Act Roles and Obligations
slide.body: Lesson 4 of 14. Footer line: Educational, not legal advice.

scenes.voiceover: In the last lesson, we saw how the Act sorts AI uses into risk tiers. Now we ask who carries the duties. This lesson is educational and is not legal advice. The exact wording of each duty is in the official text.

slide.title: Four main roles
slide.body: Supply chain left to right: Provider (develops, own name) → Importer (brings non-EU system into EU) → Distributor (e.g. reseller) → Deployer (uses under own authority)

scenes.voiceover: There are four main roles. A provider develops an AI system and places it on the market under its own name. A deployer uses an AI system under its own authority at work. An importer brings a system from a provider outside the EU onto the EU market. And a distributor, such as a reseller, makes it available.

slide.title: When a deployer becomes a provider
slide.body: Deployer icon → arrow → Provider icon. Three triggers on the arrow: own name on the system · substantial change · new purpose that makes it high-risk

scenes.voiceover: Roles can change. A deployer may be treated as a provider if it puts its own name on a high-risk system, makes a substantial change to it, or changes its purpose so that it becomes high-risk.

slide.title: Provider duties (high-risk)
slide.body: Risk management · Data governance and bias checks · Technical documentation and instructions for use · Automatic logging · Human oversight by design · Accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity

scenes.voiceover: Providers of high-risk systems carry the heaviest duties. At a high level, these include risk management across the system's life, data governance with checks for bias, technical documentation and instructions for use, automatic logging, design for human oversight, and appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity.

slide.title: Provider duties (continued)
slide.body: Quality management system · Conformity assessment before launch · Registration where required · Post-market monitoring

scenes.voiceover: Providers also need a quality management system, a conformity assessment before launch, registration where required, and monitoring after the system is on the market.

slide.title: Deployer duties (high-risk)
slide.body: Use as instructed · Trained human oversight · Relevant input data · Monitor and report serious problems · Keep own logs · Inform affected people where required

scenes.voiceover: Deployers have lighter duties, but they are real. They must use the system as instructed, assign trained people to oversee it, make sure the input data they control is relevant, monitor it, report serious problems, keep the logs they control and inform affected people where required.
The Act also sets penalties for breaches, and supervision is shared between EU and national levels. Never quote penalty figures from memory. Always check the relevant provision in the official text.

scenes.stock_query: technician inspecting elevator in office building
scenes.voiceover: Think of a lift in an office building. The manufacturer must design it safely, test it and provide a manual. The building owner must use it as the manual says and arrange inspections. If the owner rebuilds the motor, the owner starts to carry some of the manufacturer's responsibility.

slide.title: One tool, three organisations
slide.body: Triage-support tool icon in the centre, labelled 'assumed high-risk'. Three spokes: Valencia vendor · Utrecht hospital · Lagos data science company

scenes.voiceover: Now let's follow one product through three fictional organisations. It is a triage-support tool that ranks hospital patients by urgency. For this example, we assume the tool is high-risk.

slide.title: Lucía · Valencia vendor
slide.body: Role: Provider. Why: built it, sells under own brand. Duties: the full provider list, from risk management to post-market monitoring

scenes.voiceover: Lucía Ferrer leads compliance at a software vendor in Valencia, Spain, which built the tool and sells it under its own brand. Her company is the provider. It carries the full list, from risk management and data governance to conformity assessment and monitoring after launch.

slide.title: Pieter · Utrecht hospital
slide.body: Role: Deployer (and GDPR controller). Why: bought and uses it. Duties: use as instructed · trained oversight · check input data · monitor · report serious incidents

scenes.voiceover: Pieter de Vries is the data protection officer at a hospital in Utrecht, in the Netherlands, which buys the tool. The hospital is a deployer. It must use the tool as instructed, assign trained staff to oversee its output, check input data, monitor it and report serious incidents. It is also a GDPR controller for patient data.

slide.title: Emeka · Lagos company
slide.body: Role: Provider outside the EU. Why: builds and sells to EU clinics. Extra: may need an EU authorised representative (to confirm). Record: role · reason · source

scenes.voiceover: Emeka Nwosu runs a data science company in Lagos that builds a similar tool and sells it directly to clinics in the EU. His company is a provider from outside the EU, so it may need an authorised representative in the EU. Each organisation writes down its role, the reason and its source.

scenes.on_screen_text: Buying a system does not remove duties.
scenes.voiceover: A common mistake is to say, the vendor is responsible for compliance. The provider carries the heaviest duties, but deployers have their own. And a deployer that customises or rebrands a system may become a provider. Check your role for each system, and check again whenever you change how you use it.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Duties follow role; one organisation can hold several. 2. High-risk providers carry the heaviest duties. 3. Deployers have duties too, and can become providers.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, duties depend on role: provider, deployer, importer or distributor, and one organisation can hold more than one. Second, providers of high-risk systems carry the heaviest duties, such as risk management, data governance, documentation, logging and human oversight. Third, deployers have their own duties, and can become providers through rebranding or substantial changes.

slide.title: Your exercise
slide.body: Same three organisations, new product: job-applicant screening tool · Likely role + reason · 3 to 5 main duties · One 'what would change our role?' note · About 25 minutes

scenes.voiceover: In the exercise below this video, you will take today's three organisations, but change the product to a tool that screens job applicants. For each one, write its likely role, three to five main duties in plain words, and one note on what would change its role.
In the next lesson, we put this together by classifying an AI system step by step. See you there.
